Daniel’s contrast between “words = abstract” and “games/pictures = embodied” is intuitively appealing, but it smuggles in a big hidden assumption: that *medium* determines “first glance” impact more than *craft* does. The lever in his example is not merely interactivity; it’s specificity—concrete scenes, constraints, and a paced sequence that forces attention. A tightly written vignette can be equally “embodied” (fiction routinely achieves this through focalization, sensory detail, and second-person address), while a game can be highly abstract (many communicate primarily through systems rather than depiction). Put differently, Daniel is circling Marshall McLuhan’s point that the medium shapes attention and participation, but he overstates it as a near-law about abstraction rather than a probabilistic tendency mediated by design choices ([Understanding Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understanding_Media)).  

Relatedly, Daniel says removing the game would leave “some general abstract story of societal uninclusiveness,” as if reader detachment were the default for text. That may be true of *didactic* text, but it’s not true of narrative as such; identification often comes from character particularity and voice, not from pixels. If the flash game he remembers is the frequently cited *Dys4ia* (uncertain, but it fits his description), its force comes from compressing micro-frustrations into mechanics—waiting, failing, being blocked—which is a kind of argument made by rules. That’s less “pictures” than what Ian Bogost calls *procedural rhetoric*: systems persuading by letting you feel how constraints operate ([Persuasive Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persuasive_Games)).  

Finally, Daniel’s closing claim that games/pictures are “generally bad at conveying abstract ideas” is only true if “abstract” means “propositional statements.” Games rarely *say* abstractions; they *instantiate* them—tradeoffs, incentives, double binds, category policing—often more directly than a paragraph can. The sharper takeaway might be: words excel at explicit propositions; games excel at making constraints legible through experience; and both can do the other job when the author builds the right scaffolding.
